slides.notes: Draws on Issues with CPAT and Options for Remediation (first presented April 2026), the Coded CPAT and other AI tools plan (September 2026) and the FY27 work plan.

slides.title: Contents — Purpose: agree the plan for rebuilding CPAT's engine with AI, in code and in Excel, and decide which smaller products to keep alongside it.

bullets.text: Why a patch is not enough

What to keep and what to drop

slides.title: PART 1 · THE PROBLEM — CPAT's mitigation module has three problems

bullets.text: The module is large, slow, heavy and hard to maintain. No user can understand or validate 250,000+ spreadsheet cells.
The WB side has not published CPAT. The IMF publication relies mostly on an elasticity meta-analysis.
A few bugs, and hard to demonstrate: it can take ten minutes to load. This limits its use in country work.

slides.title: PART 1 · MAIN CODING ISSUES — Heavy, slow and hard to keep consistent

bullets.text: Not fit for the new UI
The mitigation module is the largest part of CPAT.
Other modules depend on it, so they wait for it.
250,000+ cells are hard to understand and validate.
Excel, Python CPAT and documentation drift apart; a spreadsheet is hard to publish in a peer-reviewed journal.
Policy mixes need every sector and fuel combination handled properly: a fully consistent approach.

slides.title: PART 1 · WHY A PATCH IS NOT ENOUGH — Patching the old Excel will not be enough

bullets.text: So: rebuild the engine with AI, in code and in Excel, and keep them equal.
A new engine tab in legacy CPAT
Lambda functions, arrays and simpler prices. Result: a more consistent engine, but CPAT not much faster or smaller.
What the engine must now do
Policy mixes across every sector, fuel and policy
A clean back end for the new WB–IMF interface
GHG accounting, with every figure traceable

slides.title: PART 2 · TWO PRODUCTS, COMPARED — One set of equations, two forms

rows: What it is
The core engine in Python, with an online Shiny interface
A cut-down CPAT in Excel, built from scratch with AI
First uses
Model comparison; full country work once complete; SiSePuede and pathways tool
GHG accounting; a clean back end for the new WB–IMF interface
Users
Modelers and teams who run code; web users via Shiny
Economists who work in Excel; IMF and WB CPAT teams
Strength
Scales, tests and links to other Python models
Familiar, transparent cell by cell, easy to audit
Limit
Not open to non-coders without Shiny
Harder to scale; LAMBDA needs a recent Excel

slides.notes: Both forms share one set of equations and are kept equivalent by script. Each is built component by component, together: distribution, mitigation basics, power, other mitigation and GDP, air pollution, transport.

slides.title: PART 2 · THE CASE FOR AI-EXCEL — AI-Excel serves three purposes

bullets.text: Agreed with Dirk: a contributor to future development, not yet the full CPAT. A base for one maintainable model.
A transparent Excel tool for ex-ante DPF accounting and crediting, where each figure is traceable.
An independent check on the coded engine and on legacy CPAT. Differences point to errors on either side.

slides.notes: AI-Excel also lowers the risk of building a new user interface on an archaic back end. It is not meant to replace legacy CPAT yet; that is for later discussion.

slides.title: PART 2 · MAINTAINABILITY — Scripts keep code, Excel and docs equal

bullets.text: Claude builds the Excel through a Python script. We save (a) that full script and (b) a readable pseudocode version that produces it.
Pull data out, with a source trail
Any AI coding tool can pick it up. Proprietary data stays ring-fenced outside the shared files.

slides.notes: Joint working with AI: rather than passing around long context, we keep small generative files and concise scripts. Anyone, with any AI tool, can regenerate the Excel, the code and the documentation from them.

slides.title: PART 2 · ISSUES AND RESOLUTIONS — The main risks are known and manageable

rows: IMF ownership
The IMF may want to take control, and could build its own version.
Agree the WB side first, then bring the IMF in early. Their version may look like ours.
Compatibility
LAMBDA functions need recent Excel; older copies, e.g. in finance ministries, may fail.
Finance ministries are not the first audience. LAMBDAs can be turned back into direct formulae.
Functionality
Excel CPAT holds many ad hoc changes; the new model will not match them all at first.
Build a sound, maintainable base; extend it once code and AI-Excel are adequate.
Scope
Risk of two Excel models to maintain in the long run.
A contributor to the WB–IMF process, not yet the full CPAT. Long-term, keep one Excel.
Accessibility
Teams use different AI tools, and some data is proprietary.
Works with Claude or GitHub Copilot; proprietary data kept ring-fenced.

slides.notes: Ask the room: what other issues should we plan for? These points come from discussion with Dirk.

slides.title: PART 3 · B · SINGLE PYTHON PLATFORM — Make existing models easy to use, not develop them further

bullets.text: CPAT, MFMod-Python and FTT, as they are today, on one common platform.
A shared set-up and one user guide. FTT made ready to run, with data aligned to CPAT countries.
No further model development, and no full merging of FTT or MFMod into CPAT.

slides.title: PART 3 · C · POLICY ISSUE REPORT — One issue, one country, for example feebates

bullets.text: Where the country stands on the issue, drawn from the dashboard and diagnostic.
The best policy design, and what other countries did and learned.
The opportunities for reform in that country, and how to get there.

slides.notes: The dashboard says what is there; the policy issue report says what to do next. Together they give a fast, sourced starting point for policy dialogue.

Shown alongside the macro-fiscal and tax indicators.

slides.title: PART 4 · WHAT TO KEEP AND WHAT TO DROP — The plan is full to 20 March: anything added must replace something

bullets.text: Coded CPAT and AI-Excel. Funded; the base for everything else
GHG accounting. A corporate requirement; no DPF tool exists
Dashboard and policy report. Prototypes exist; funding to confirm
Policy crediting and FFI. One week, on GHG accounting
Total Carbon Price into GHG accounting. Not yet scheduled
Energy GP code help. Not on the timeline; needs a slot
Patching legacy Excel (new tab, Lambdas): superseded
Full CPAT replacement; merging FTT or MFMod: later
April items not in FY27 plan: ETS pilot, downstream pricing, CPAT paper

slides.source: Source: FY27 work plan v1.1 (28 Sept 2026)
slides.notes: For discussion. The work plan selects GHG accounting (3a) and marks policy crediting (3b) and the tax/fiscal dashboard (3c) as possibly dropped, at five weeks each. The master timeline gives them much less: one week for policy crediting and FFI, two weeks each for the dashboard and policy reports. The Energy GP coding help (3d, two weeks) is in the work plan but not on the master timeline, so it needs a slot or should go. The April items (ETS pilot, downstream industrial pricing, CPAT working paper) do not appear in the FY27 plan; confirm whether they are done, handed over or dropped.
